question: An aerodynamic stall occurs when:

options.text: The airspeed drops below a fixed value printed in the aircraft's flight manual
The angle of attack exceeds the wing's critical (stalling) angle of attack, causing the airflow to separate
The engine loses power, regardless of angle of attack
The aircraft descends below its minimum safe altitude

explanation: A stall is fundamentally an angle-of-attack event, not an airspeed event: it occurs whenever the critical angle of attack is exceeded and the airflow separates from the upper surface, causing a sudden loss of lift. A published stalling speed is only the speed at which this angle is reached in one specific set of conditions.

question: In a level turn at a bank angle producing a load factor of 2g, how does the stalling speed compare with straight-and-level flight?

options.text: It is unchanged, since stalling speed does not depend on load factor
It increases by the square root of the load factor — about 1.41 times higher
It decreases, because the wings are generating more lift in the turn
It doubles exactly, in direct proportion to the load factor

explanation: Stalling speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor, because the wing must reach the same critical angle of attack at a higher speed to support the increased load. At 2g, stalling speed rises by the square root of 2, about 41%, over the 1g stalling speed.

question: If an aircraft's weight increases by 21% for a given flight, its stalling speed in the same configuration will:

options.text: Increase by approximately 10%, since stalling speed varies with the square root of weight
Increase by exactly 21%, in direct proportion to weight
Decrease, because a heavier aircraft requires a lower angle of attack
Remain unchanged, since stalling speed depends only on angle of attack

explanation: Because lift at the stall must equal weight, and lift varies with the square of speed at a fixed angle of attack, stalling speed varies with the square root of weight. A 21% increase in weight corresponds to a factor of the square root of 1.21, or 1.1 — an approximate 10% increase in stalling speed.

question: The purpose of a stall warning device, such as a stick shaker or an aural warning based on sensed angle of attack, is to:

options.text: Automatically recover the aircraft from a fully developed stall
Alert the pilot that the wing is approaching its critical angle of attack, before the stall actually occurs
Prevent the aircraft from descending below a set altitude
Indicate that the aircraft has exceeded its maximum operating speed

explanation: Stall warning systems are set to trigger at a small margin of angle of attack before the actual critical angle is reached, giving the pilot advance warning to reduce angle of attack before the stall develops. They warn of an approaching condition; they do not by themselves recover the aircraft.

question: Ice accumulation on the leading edge of a wing typically affects its stalling behaviour by:

options.text: Increasing the critical angle of attack and lowering the stalling speed
Having no aerodynamic effect until a significant thickness has built up
Disrupting airflow over the upper surface, which reduces the critical angle of attack and increases stalling speed
Only affecting drag, never lift or stall characteristics

explanation: Even small amounts of ice roughen and distort the leading edge, disturbing the smooth airflow needed to reach high angles of attack. This typically reduces the critical angle of attack at which the wing stalls and increases stalling speed, often with little warning from the aircraft's normal stall warning system.

question: Many wings are designed with "washout", a reduction in angle of incidence from root to tip, mainly so that:

options.text: The wingtip stalls before the wing root, keeping the ailerons effective for as long as possible
The wing root stalls before the wingtip, keeping the ailerons effective for as long as possible
Induced drag is eliminated entirely
The aircraft's cruise speed is increased

explanation: Washout gives the wing root a higher angle of attack than the tip at any given moment, so the root reaches its critical angle of attack and stalls first. This keeps the outboard section of the wing — and the ailerons mounted on it — flying and effective into the early stages of a stall.

question: An "accelerated stall" occurs when:

options.text: The aircraft stalls at a speed higher than the normal 1g stalling speed, due to a load factor greater than one, such as in a steep turn or abrupt pull-up
The aircraft stalls only at very low airspeed
The throttle is advanced to full power during the stall
The aircraft exceeds its never-exceed speed

explanation: "Accelerated" refers to the increased load factor, not to airspeed increasing: any manoeuvre that raises load factor above 1g raises the angle of attack needed to sustain it, so the critical angle of attack — and therefore the stall — is reached at a correspondingly higher airspeed.

question: A "secondary stall" is:

options.text: A stall that occurs a second time during the same flight, for unrelated reasons
A stall induced by an abrupt or premature recovery attempt from an initial stall, before sufficient airspeed has been regained
A stall that only affects the horizontal stabilizer
A stall from which recovery is never possible

explanation: A secondary stall happens when a pilot raises the nose again too soon during recovery from an initial stall, before the wing has regained enough airspeed to sustain the resulting angle of attack — stalling the wing a second time as a direct result of the recovery technique itself.

question: Which of the following is a typical aerodynamic symptom of an approaching stall, as distinct from an artificial stall warning device?

options.text: An increase in control effectiveness
Buffet caused by separated, turbulent airflow striking the tailplane or fuselage, and reduced control effectiveness
A sudden increase in airspeed
An automatic decrease in angle of attack

explanation: As the wing approaches its critical angle of attack, airflow begins separating naturally, and the resulting turbulent wake can buffet the tailplane or aft fuselage. Control surfaces immersed in this disturbed, slower-moving air also become less effective — both genuine aerodynamic warning signs, independent of any electronic or mechanical stall warning system.

question: An aerodynamic spin is best described as:

options.text: A rapid roll with the wings still flying normally
An autorotation following a stall, in which one wing is more deeply stalled than the other, combined with yaw
A steep spiral dive with the wings unstalled and airspeed increasing
A manoeuvre that can only happen at high airspeed

explanation: A spin requires the wing to already be stalled. One wing then becomes more deeply stalled than the other — often because of yaw at the stall — producing an asymmetric lift and drag condition that sustains a combined rolling, yawing, pitching autorotation, quite different from an unstalled spiral dive.

question: During the autorotative phase of a spin, the more deeply stalled, descending wing continues to auto-rotate mainly because:

options.text: It is producing more lift than the rising wing
Its effective angle of attack is even further past the stall, so it produces less lift and more drag than the rising wing, sustaining the rotation
Engine torque forces it downward
The ailerons are held fully deflected by the pilot throughout

explanation: The descending wing's downward motion adds to its angle of attack, driving it deeper into the stalled region of the lift curve where lift falls and drag rises further. The rising wing, meanwhile, sees a reduced angle of attack and produces relatively more lift and less drag — the asymmetry that keeps the rotation going on its own.

question: Aircraft with a T-tail configuration are particularly susceptible to a "deep stall" because:

options.text: The horizontal stabilizer is mounted low, ahead of the wing
At a high angle of attack, the turbulent, separated wake from the stalled wing can blanket the high-mounted horizontal stabilizer, severely reducing or eliminating elevator (pitch-down) authority
T-tails have no elevator at all
T-tails always stall at a lower angle of attack than a conventional tail

explanation: With the horizontal stabilizer mounted at the top of the fin, a sufficiently high angle of attack can place it directly in the wing's stalled, turbulent wake. If that happens, elevator authority to lower the nose can be badly degraded exactly when it is needed most — the mechanism behind a "deep stall" or "super-stall".

question: The fundamental first action in a standard stall recovery is to:

options.text: Apply full aft control input to raise the nose immediately
Reduce the angle of attack, typically by moving the control column forward (or reducing back-pressure), to unstall the wing before addressing power or altitude
Apply full rudder in the direction of the low wing
Retract the flaps immediately, regardless of airspeed

explanation: Because a stall is an angle-of-attack event, the only action that actually ends it is reducing angle of attack below the critical angle. Every other action — adding power, levelling the wings, managing altitude loss — matters, but comes after (or alongside) that first, essential step.

question: Compared with an aft center of gravity, a more forward center of gravity generally makes an aircraft:

options.text: More prone to entering and sustaining a spin
More resistant to stalling and spinning, though it also raises stalling speed slightly and requires more elevator authority to reach the critical angle of attack
Unaffected in its stall characteristics
Unable to stall at all

explanation: A forward center of gravity increases the tailplane's stabilising moment arm and generally makes the aircraft more resistant to reaching, and sustaining, a stalled or spinning condition — one reason aft CG limits exist. The trade-off is a slightly higher stalling speed and a greater elevator deflection needed to reach the critical angle of attack.

question: An angle-of-attack limiting ("stall protection" or "alpha protection") system, found on some modern aircraft, works by:

options.text: Automatically preventing the pilot's control input from commanding an angle of attack beyond a protected limit
Only sounding a warning, with no actual limiting of control authority
Increasing the aircraft's critical angle of attack permanently
Disconnecting the elevator entirely near the stall

explanation: Rather than simply warning the pilot, an angle-of-attack protection system limits how much elevator authority is available as the wing approaches its protected angle of attack, so that ordinary control inputs — even full aft stick — cannot command the aircraft past that protected limit under normal operation.

question: An engine nacelle or pylon mounted on or ahead of the wing can affect local stalling behaviour mainly because it:

options.text: Disturbs the local airflow over the wing immediately behind it, sometimes promoting earlier local separation in that area
Always delays the stall over the whole wing
Has no aerodynamic interaction with the wing at all
Only affects engine cooling, never the wing's airflow

explanation: A nacelle or pylon interrupts and disturbs the otherwise smooth airflow reaching the wing section immediately behind it, which can promote earlier local boundary layer separation in that region — a real interference effect that designers sometimes address with local vortex generators or a shaped fairing.

question: On a propeller aircraft, a power-on stall typically occurs at a lower indicated airspeed than an equivalent power-off stall mainly because:

options.text: The propeller slipstream over the wing root area increases local dynamic pressure and can alter the effective local angle of attack, and the thrust vector itself also has a small vertical lift component at a high pitch attitude
Power has no aerodynamic effect on the wing whatsoever
Power-on stalls always occur at a higher airspeed than power-off stalls
Adding power always increases stalling speed

explanation: With power applied, the slipstream-washed portion of the wing sees higher dynamic pressure and altered local flow, and at the high pitch attitude typical of a power-on stall entry, part of the thrust vector itself acts upward — both effects that let the aircraft reach the stall at a lower indicated airspeed than in the equivalent power-off condition.

question: Flying through turbulence close to an aircraft's normal stalling speed carries extra risk mainly because:

options.text: A sudden gust can momentarily add enough angle of attack to exceed the critical angle, triggering a stall at an indicated airspeed above the smooth-air stalling speed
Turbulence always reduces angle of attack, making a stall less likely
Turbulence has no effect on angle of attack at all
Turbulence only affects heading, never angle of attack

explanation: A vertical gust momentarily changes the relative airflow direction and therefore the wing's effective angle of attack, independent of airspeed or pilot input. In turbulence, this can push angle of attack past the critical value — and trigger a stall — at an indicated airspeed noticeably higher than the smooth-air 1g stalling speed, which is exactly why extra speed margin is recommended in turbulent conditions.

question: A "cross-control" (skidding) stall — entered with opposite aileron and rudder applied, such as in an overshooting base-to-final turn — is especially hazardous because:

options.text: It stalls the wing symmetrically, with no tendency to drop either wing
The resulting yaw and uncoordinated airflow can stall one wing well before the other, dropping that wing sharply and often triggering a spin entry, close to the ground
It can only happen at high altitude
It never involves rudder input at all

explanation: Crossed controls produce a skid, and the resulting sideslip and yaw distort the airflow so that one wing reaches its critical angle of attack well before the other. That wing drops sharply, often rolling the aircraft toward an incipient spin — a scenario made especially dangerous during a low, close-to-the-ground turn such as base-to-final, where there is little altitude to recover.

question: An "incipient" spin, as distinct from a fully developed one, refers to:

options.text: The first part of the spin, roughly the first couple of turns, before rotation and descent rates have stabilised — generally the easier phase in which to recover
A spin that has already fully stabilised and is harder to stop
A spin that only happens in gliders
A spin entered deliberately for aerobatic display only

explanation: During the incipient phase, the aerodynamic and inertial forces driving the spin have not yet reached a stable balance, and recovery inputs are generally more effective and the aircraft responds more readily than once the spin has fully developed and stabilised — which is why prompt recognition and early recovery action matter.

question: The standard control input sequence taught for recovering from an established spin is generally:

options.text: Power to idle, ailerons neutral, full rudder opposite to the direction of rotation, then forward elevator to break the stall, followed by neutralising the rudder as rotation stops and easing out of the resulting dive
Full aft elevator held throughout, with ailerons used to stop the rotation
Full power applied immediately, with no other control input
Rudder applied in the same direction as the rotation

explanation: The generally taught sequence closes the throttle (removing any asymmetric power effect), neutralises ailerons (which can otherwise aggravate the spin), applies rudder opposite to the rotation to stop the yaw, then moves the elevator forward to reduce angle of attack and break the stall — only after which the dive that follows is eased out of.

question: In a spin, the aircraft rotates:

options.text: In the direction of the more deeply stalled, lower wing
Always to the right, regardless of which wing drops
In the direction of the higher, less-stalled wing
Randomly, with no relationship to which wing is more stalled

explanation: The wing that is more deeply stalled produces less lift and more drag than the other, and this asymmetry is what drives the autorotation — so the spin rotates toward whichever wing is the more stalled, lower one, not the reverse.

question: If one wing drops at the stall, the generally correct pilot response is to:

options.text: Immediately apply aileron toward the high wing to force the wings level
Avoid using aileron to lift the dropped wing, and instead reduce angle of attack, using rudder as needed, since aileron can further stall (and increase drag on) the already lower wing
Apply full power with no other change
Pull further back on the controls to raise the nose

explanation: Deflecting aileron to raise a dropped wing at the stall increases that wing's effective angle of attack further (and adds induced drag on it), which can deepen the stall on that side and worsen the wing drop rather than correcting it. The safer response is to reduce angle of attack first, and use rudder rather than aileron to help keep the aircraft coordinated.

question: A stall entered from a climbing turn tends to be more abrupt than one entered from straight-and-level flight mainly because:

options.text: The turn combines an already elevated angle of attack from the climb with the increased load factor of the turn, and any asymmetry between the inside and outside wing can produce a sharper break
Climbing turns always occur at a lower angle of attack than level flight
A climbing turn eliminates load factor entirely
Climbing turns cannot produce a stall at all

explanation: A climbing turn already asks for a higher angle of attack than level flight, and the turn itself adds load factor on top of that. Any asymmetry between the inside and outside wing's local angle of attack in the turn can then produce a more sudden, more pronounced wing drop than a comparable straight-ahead stall.

question: Beyond its effect on how easily a spin is entered, an aft center of gravity also affects spin recovery because it can:

options.text: Flatten the spin (raise the nose attitude during rotation) and reduce elevator authority to break the stall, making recovery slower or, in extreme cases, impossible
Always make the spin easier to recover from
Have no effect on the spin once it has already been entered
Automatically stop the rotation on its own

explanation: An aft center of gravity can shift a spin toward a flatter attitude, with the nose higher relative to the horizon during rotation, while also reducing the elevator's effectiveness at generating the forward pitching moment needed to break the stall — a combination that can make recovery markedly slower, or in a sufficiently aft-loaded aircraft, essentially unrecoverable within the aft CG range that is meant to be avoided for exactly this reason.

question: An ice-induced "tailplane stall", distinct from a wing stall, occurs when:

options.text: Ice disrupts airflow over the horizontal stabilizer enough that it loses its needed lift (or download), often triggered or worsened by flap extension increasing downwash on the tail — and the correct response is opposite to a normal wing stall, generally retracting flap and easing (not pulling) on the controls
The wing, not the tail, always stalls first regardless of ice
It is recovered from in exactly the same way as an ordinary wing stall
It can only happen with the landing gear retracted

explanation: Because many tailplanes fly at a negative angle of attack producing a download to balance the aircraft, ice contaminating the tailplane can cause it to lose that download suddenly — often precipitated by extending flaps, which increases downwash reaching the tail. A tailplane stall produces an uncommanded pitch-down, and the recommended response (retract flap, ease rather than pull on the controls) is the opposite of a normal wing-stall recovery, which is exactly why correctly identifying which surface has stalled matters.

question: A "whip stall" (tuck-under) occurs when:

options.text: An aircraft climbs steeply enough (as at the top of a zoom climb) that airspeed decays toward zero, and the nose then drops or "tucks" abruptly as the wing and tail lose effectiveness together
It happens only in level, unaccelerated cruise flight
It is identical in every respect to a normal, gentle 1g stall
It only occurs at very high indicated airspeed

explanation: At the top of a steep climb or zoom, airspeed can decay toward zero before the aircraft has time to settle into a normal stall break, and the resulting loss of both wing lift and tail effectiveness together can produce an abrupt, whipping nose-down pitching motion — a distinct and more violent event than an ordinary stall entered at a controlled airspeed.

question: On a multi-engine aircraft, if the published minimum control speed with one engine inoperative (VMC) is higher than the aircraft's stalling speed in that configuration, the effective minimum safe speed is:

options.text: The stalling speed, since VMC is never relevant once above the stall
VMC itself, since directional control could be lost at that speed even though the wing has not yet stalled
Always exactly halfway between the two speeds
Irrelevant, since only single-engine aircraft can stall

explanation: VMC and the stall are two entirely different limits — one aerodynamic (the wing), one about yaw control authority against asymmetric thrust. Whichever of the two is reached first, at the higher speed, becomes the effective floor: if VMC is above stalling speed, directional control can be lost before the wing itself stalls, which is precisely why VMC is published and respected as its own limit.

question: Compared with a clean-configuration stall, a full-flap stall on some aircraft can be noticeably more abrupt because:

options.text: Flap deployment can change the spanwise pattern in which the wing separates, sometimes reducing the natural stall-warning margin the clean wing would otherwise give
Flaps always make every stall gentler with no exception
Flaps eliminate the possibility of a wing drop entirely
Flap position has no bearing on stall character at all

explanation: Because flaps change the local pressure distribution and camber, they can also change how and where separation first develops across the span, and on some aircraft this shifts the stall toward a sharper, less-warned break with full flap compared with the clean wing — a real, aircraft-specific difference worth knowing rather than assuming flaps always make a stall gentler.

question: During the landing flare, ground effect's reduction of induced drag and change in lift can mean that, for the same indicated airspeed and control input as out of ground effect, the aircraft:

options.text: Can hold a given height a little longer, effectively extending the margin before reaching the stalling angle of attack
Always stalls at a noticeably higher airspeed near the ground
Is completely unaffected by proximity to the ground
Becomes impossible to stall while within ground effect

explanation: Ground effect's reduction in induced drag and downwash effectively increases lift for a given angle of attack close to the surface, which is part of why an aircraft can "float" during flare — extending, though not eliminating, the margin before the critical angle of attack is reached at that lower height.

subtopic: Aft CG and Stall Break Sharpness
question: Beyond raising stall risk generally, an aft center of gravity can also make the stall break itself sharper mainly because:

options.text: There is less of the natural nose-down pitching tendency that a more forward CG provides once the critical angle of attack is exceeded
An aft CG always makes the stall gentler and better warned
CG position has no bearing on how the stall itself feels
An aft CG increases the critical angle of attack

explanation: With the center of gravity further aft, there is less of a nose-down pitching moment naturally available once the wing stalls, so the aircraft is less inclined to pitch its own nose down and reduce angle of attack on its own — often producing a sharper, more sustained stall break than the same aircraft with a more forward CG.

question: A wing can also stall under sustained negative g (such as in inverted or strongly nose-down manoeuvring), which happens when:

options.text: The angle of attack becomes sufficiently negative to exceed the wing's negative critical angle of attack, on the opposite side of the lift curve from a normal stall
It is aerodynamically impossible for a wing to stall under negative g
It only ever happens at exactly the same angle of attack as a normal positive stall
It requires the aircraft to be flying backward

explanation: Just as a wing stalls when angle of attack exceeds a positive critical value, it can also stall on the negative side of the lift curve if angle of attack becomes sufficiently negative — relevant to aerobatic and inverted flight, and part of why aircraft cleared for sustained inverted flight need systems (such as inverted fuel and oil systems) built around that possibility.

question: "Low-speed buffet onset" refers to:

options.text: The angle of attack at which the first noticeable buffet appears, slightly before the full critical angle of attack is reached, giving a natural pre-stall margin
Exactly the same angle of attack as the full stall, with no distinction
A phenomenon that only appears at high Mach number
A margin that exists only when an artificial stall warning system is installed

explanation: As angle of attack approaches the critical value, localised separation begins producing buffet before the wing is actually fully stalled. This low-speed buffet onset is a genuine aerodynamic margin ahead of the full stall — distinct from an artificial warning device, though many aircraft also carry one for a more definite alert.

question: Retracting flaps immediately after recovering from a stall at low altitude is generally inadvisable because:

options.text: It reduces CLmax and raises stalling speed at exactly the moment altitude and airspeed margins are already reduced
Flap position has no effect on stalling speed
Retracting flaps always increases lift immediately
It is required by every recovery procedure regardless of altitude

explanation: Flaps lower stalling speed and raise CLmax; retracting them straight after a low-altitude stall recovery removes that safety margin right when the aircraft has the least altitude and speed cushion to spare, which is why flap retraction is normally sequenced only once a safe altitude and airspeed have been re-established.

question: On a multi-engine aircraft with wing-mounted engines, losing one engine can affect stall margin because:

options.text: The loss of that engine's slipstream over the affected wing section, combined with the bank and rudder needed to control the resulting yaw, changes the effective stalling behaviour compared with all-engines-operating flight
Losing an engine has no effect on stalling behaviour whatsoever
It always lowers the stalling speed
It only affects the tailplane, never the wing

explanation: An inoperative wing-mounted engine removes that engine's slipstream energisation of the local wing area, while the bank and rudder used to control the resulting asymmetric thrust change the effective local angle of attack across the span — both of which alter stalling behaviour from the symmetric, all-engines-operating case.

question: Encountering a preceding aircraft's wake turbulence can produce an unexpected approach to the stall mainly because:

options.text: The rotational airflow in a trailing wingtip vortex can abruptly change the local angle of attack on one or both wings with no warning
Wake turbulence always reduces angle of attack safely
Wake turbulence has no aerodynamic effect on angle of attack
It can only affect an aircraft flying directly behind and below the generating aircraft's exact altitude

explanation: The rotating airflow inside a wingtip vortex can suddenly and unpredictably add or subtract angle of attack on whichever part of the wing it strikes, with essentially no warning, which is why wake turbulence encounters are treated as a genuine upset risk and why appropriate separation from a preceding aircraft is maintained.

question: Flight manuals sometimes publish both a power-off and a power-on stalling speed for the same weight and configuration mainly because:

options.text: The two genuinely differ, since slipstream and thrust-vector effects at power mean the aircraft can reach the critical angle of attack at a different indicated airspeed than with power off
The two figures are always identical and the distinction is purely for legal purposes
Only the power-off figure is ever aerodynamically meaningful
Power-on stalling speed is never published in practice

explanation: Because slipstream and thrust-vector effects genuinely change the airspeed at which the critical angle of attack is reached, the power-on and power-off stalling speeds for the same configuration and weight can differ meaningfully — which is why both are sometimes published rather than assuming one figure covers both cases.

question: An asymmetric fuel load or uneven icing between the two wings can cause a stall to result in:

options.text: A symmetric stall with no tendency to drop either wing
One wing reaching its critical angle of attack, or losing lift, before the other, producing a wing-drop rather than a straight-ahead break
No stall at all, regardless of angle of attack
A change in stalling speed but never in which wing stalls first

explanation: Any asymmetry between the two wings — an uneven fuel load changing local weight distribution and structural twist, or ice accreting unevenly — can mean one side reaches its critical angle of attack, or loses lift, slightly before the other, producing a wing-drop stall rather than a clean, symmetric break.

question: "Wing rock" near the stall refers to:

options.text: A single, committed drop of one wing that does not recover on its own
An oscillatory rolling motion, alternating from one wing to the other, caused by unstable, alternating separation near maximum lift coefficient
A phenomenon that only ever occurs well below the critical angle of attack
A rolling motion caused exclusively by rudder input

explanation: Near maximum lift coefficient, flow separation on each wing can alternate in an unstable way, first favouring one side and then the other, producing a repeated rocking roll motion rather than a single, committed drop toward one wing — a distinct phenomenon from a one-wing-low stall, sometimes seen on swept or delta-shaped planforms at high angle of attack.

question: As altitude increases, an aircraft's stalling speed expressed in calibrated (or indicated) airspeed:

options.text: Stays essentially the same, since the critical angle of attack and lift coefficient at the stall are unchanged
Increases steadily with altitude
Decreases steadily with altitude
Becomes undefined above 10,000 feet

explanation: Calibrated airspeed already reflects dynamic pressure the same way at any altitude, and since the critical angle of attack (and the lift coefficient at which the stall occurs) does not change with altitude, stalling speed in calibrated airspeed terms stays essentially constant. Stalling speed in true airspeed terms, by contrast, does increase with altitude, since more true airspeed is needed to produce the same dynamic pressure in the thinner air.

question: On a typical single-engine, propeller-driven aircraft with a clockwise-rotating engine (as seen from the cockpit), approaching a stall at high power and low airspeed can produce a tendency to:

options.text: Drop the left wing and yaw left, from the combined effect of torque reaction, P-factor and slipstream at high power and high angle of attack
Drop the right wing exclusively, with no left-turning tendency at all
Remain perfectly symmetric regardless of power setting
Yaw right only, never left

explanation: At high power and low airspeed — exactly the conditions of a power-on stall approach — torque reaction, the asymmetric blade (P-factor) effect and the slipstream's yawing tendency all combine in the same left-turning direction on a typical clockwise-rotating engine, which is why many single-engine types show a marked tendency to yaw and roll left approaching a power-on stall if uncorrected.

question: A spin is considered "fully developed" once:

options.text: Its rotation rate and rate of descent have stabilised into a steady, repeating pattern, as the aerodynamic and inertial forces involved reach equilibrium
The aircraft has completed exactly one full turn, regardless of whether anything has stabilised
The pilot has applied full recovery controls
The engine has failed

explanation: As a spin progresses beyond its initial, changing incipient phase, the aerodynamic forces from the stalled wings, the drag and inertia of the airframe, and the rotational motion settle into a repeating, steady-state pattern — a genuinely different, generally more resistant-to-recover condition than the incipient phase that preceded it.
